commenter_title: Cloud Data Engineer
comment_text: I think corporate hiring is too focused on number of years in specific technologies in a checklist approach. I like to look for the nature of the person. We had one candidate who spent evenings studying new technologies while he worked during the day. What he studied was not related to what we needed, but I felt that a guy with that drive would learn the technology we were using. He turned out to be a superb developer, and it was a pleasure to supervise him. I suggest not dismissing the technical interview too quickly. A friend was hiring an assembly language developer. They had a simple coding test with may be a 5 line answer. One candidate handed him the uncompleted test and said "Ok, you got me, I don't know anything about assembly language." And he walked out. When hiring a database administrator, I asked the candidates to explain the first three normal forms. None of the candidates could answer that question, and it was discouraging. Then, when asked the question, the next candidate stood up, grabbed a dry erase marker, went to the white board and gave a 5 minute lecture of the first three normal forms complete with diagrams. Guess who got hired? :) I have never seen anything like that before or since.

comment_text: I'll throw this in here: Often the best engineer is the one who is the best at googling / figuring it out. As an analogy, they're the one who has worked on many different jet engines in the past, doesn't know the one you're talking about all that well, but knows the predecessor or related ones and is excellent at reading the documentation, googling, asking his professional network, etc.; and within a short period of time, can become as good as any current engineer on the team. What does this analogy comprise if you break it down? 1. Familiar with the tech but not yet exact 2. Very strong ability to learn quickly 3. Very efficient at learning and figuring things out Be it systems or coding, I'll hire the person who is great at learning and getting up to speed on whatever they're given. I will not, however, try to design some interview process that gets very specific about something. I'll ask them enough depth to filter out the inexperienced and liars, and I may throw in some deep questions but I weigh those at about 10% of the decision with the bulk of the decision being this: Can this person figure out how to be as about as good as a regular team member in the first 3-6 months? Choose process over product.

comment_text: I call it the "1986 Toyota Corolla Problem" Imagine turning down a seasoned cross-country driver because they haven't specifically driven a Toyota Corolla. Sounds ridiculous, right? Yet, this is exactly what happens in IT hiring every day. Hiring managers and teams get so hyper-focused on whether a candidate has used one specific, niche tool or framework that they completely miss the bigger picture. Instead of asking, "Have you driven this exact car?" we need to be asking: "How many miles have you driven?" "Do you know how to drive a manual?" "Do you know how to read the owner's manual?" Technology changes constantly. The specific "car" your team is driving today probably won't be the one you're driving in three years. If someone is a great driver who understands the mechanics of the road and knows how to read the manual, they can drive your tech stack. Let's stop hiring for matching acronyms on a resume and start hiring for adaptability, fundamentals, and problem-solving mileage.

They learn the market, understand talent psychology, and keep refining how they engage candidates. Skills can travel. Pedigree doesn’t decide outcomes. Obsession does.

comment_text: This resonates. 11+ years in agency recruiting and business development taught me that real recruiting was never “post and pray.” It was market mapping, competitor analysis, passive outreach, and relationship building long before a job order ever hit the desk. I do think COVID accelerated a major shift. Many experienced headhunters exited the industry, teams downsized, and volume became the priority over strategy. At the same time, many organizations became heavily dependent on AI tools, resume scanning, automated rejections, workflow automation, which increased efficiency but reduced human interaction. AI should enhance recruiting, not replace discernment. When algorithms filter before a recruiter even reviews a profile, you risk missing high-potential talent. And when recruiters are buried in back-to-back meetings and administrative tasks, they don’t have the time to truly headhunt. That’s not an individual failure it’s often structural.The best recruiters still build pipelines before they’re needed. They still strategically source. They take time to study each role deeply and create intentional hiring plans. They continuously build strong relationships with candidates and clients not just when there’s an opening, but always.

At one point it became purely transactional and volume driven, which led me straight into burnout. Over time, I understood, recruiting is not about posting and waiting. It is about strategy, market mapping, competitive intelligence, understanding compensation, and being intentional about the clients and ecosystem you choose to operate in. It is also about networking with purpose and allowing yourself thinking time to analyze the market, refine your approach, and build real strategies instead of reacting. Patience is a powerful tool in this profession. Recruiting requires timing, discipline, and planning strategies. Today, working in retained executive search environment, the difference feels clear. When you operate in a true 360 full desk model, take ownership of business development, and specialize in a niche, something shifts. You start advising within a market. Recruiting is influence, intelligence, strategy, and discipline.

comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). That distinction matters because it changes expectations. ◀️ Especially at the leadership level, the meaningful success metric isn’t interview volume. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions. I cover the "talent agent" vs "talent scout" model in a Forbes Coaches Council article, Feb 2024. https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbescoachescouncil/2024/02/21/will-an-executive-recruiter-find-a-job-for-me-3-recruitment-models-and-how-to-leverage-relationships-with-recruiters/

comment_text: Great question! It’s refreshing to see someone actually reviewing PSLs with intent rather than just letting them sit there for years. From my side, having been on both sides of the fence, the agencies that tend to stay on PSLs long term usually do these things well: ** They operate with honesty and transparency. If the salary, timeline or expectations don’t align with the market, they say so early rather than quietly chasing an impossible search. ** They challenge briefs when needed. Good agencies aren’t afraid to have the difficult conversations if something isn’t realistic. ** They understand the business, not just the vacancy. The best results happen when the agency knows the culture, team dynamics and longer-term hiring plans, not just the job spec. ** They protect candidate experience. Even when someone isn’t hired, the process still reflects well on the brand. Something I think often gets overlooked is market intelligence. A good agency shouldn’t just send CVs, they should also feed back salary trends, competitor hiring activity and candidate sentiment so hiring teams can make better decisions. comment_text: If you want to gauge a firm’s ability to deliver consistent results, look past the branding and scrutinize their hiring operating system. Whether they call themselves a "recruitment agency" or a "strategic partner" is irrelevant—labels mean nothing if they cannot bridge the gap between initial intent and a confident hiring decision. Don’t be swayed by agencies that lead with "speed" in sourcing or screening. These are merely peripheral activities. They are ultimately meaningless if the firm’s internal architecture lacks a foundation of: * Upstream Alignment: Ensuring the search is calibrated before the first candidate is ever contacted. * Structured Flow: A repeatable process that maintains momentum without sacrificing quality. * Integrated Tools: Using technology to enable data-driven decisions rather than just automating spam. * Governance & Ethics: Establishing clear standards and accountability to ensure every hire is a strategic fit. True value isn't found in how fast an agency can run; it's found in the systematic infrastructure they use to ensure they are running in the right direction.
